title: Why New Remote Workers Need Experienced Teammates, Not Star Performers

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Caster Inc, a Japanese company providing online administrative and secretarial services, has never operated a single physical office. Its roughly 900 employees, spread across all 47 of Japan's prefectures and 23 other countries as of March 2025, handle client work entirely through remote communication platforms. Because the company was built from the start as a fully distributed organisation rather than converting to remote work later, it offers researchers an unusually clean setting in which to study how colleagues influence one another's output, without the complication of comparing remote staff against office-based staff.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: A team of researchers analysed 977 employee-month records from one of the company's departments, covering April 2022 through March 2023. Observations from an employee's first six months, a standard training period, were excluded so that the sample reflected only fully established staff. The dataset combined three separate internal sources: human resources records giving background details on each employee, operational logs tracking which clients each person served and how many hours they worked, and records of internal messaging activity. Combining these three sources let the researchers see not only how much each employee produced, but who they were working alongside and how often they exchanged messages with teammates in a given month.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: What made the study unusually rigorous was a quirk of company policy: new hires were placed into teams using a simple round-robin system based purely on the order in which they joined, a process neither managers nor employees could influence. This effectively randomised which colleagues an employee ended up working alongside, letting the researchers treat team composition almost as if it had been assigned in a controlled experiment, and so identify cause and effect rather than mere correlation.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Productivity was measured as the number of distinct clients an employee served in a given month. Because the company standardises working hours and each client contract allocates a fixed thirty hours of monthly support, the number of clients handled is a dependable stand-in for how much useful work an individual completed, avoiding the ambiguity that self-reported effort or hours worked can introduce into workplace research.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The first result ran against a common assumption. Working alongside colleagues who were themselves highly productive produced no measurable improvement in an individual's own output, even for employees placed in teams whose average productivity ranked in the top quarter of the company. Whatever benefit workers usually gain from watching or being motivated by star performers, it did not appear here.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Experience, rather than raw productivity, turned out to matter a great deal. Employees placed in teams with the most experienced average tenure, the top twenty-five per cent of teams by this measure, saw their own productivity rise by roughly 12.2 per cent. This benefit was strongly concentrated among newer staff: employees in their first year on the job gained around 26.2 per cent when surrounded by experienced teammates, second-year employees gained a more modest 8.6 per cent, and the effect shrank close to zero for longer-serving staff.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: A further finding complicated the obvious explanation that experienced teams simply talk to one another more. In fact, teams with the highest average tenure communicated internally less than other teams, a statistically significant difference, and experienced or already highly productive employees tended to perform best in exactly these lower-communication settings, suggesting that frequent messaging may sometimes distract rather than assist workers who already know what they are doing.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: The researchers interpret the pattern through the idea of a transactive memory system, in which effective teams develop a shared, largely implicit sense of who knows what, letting members find the right person to ask rather than needing constant interaction. In an office, visibly high-performing colleagues can motivate others through social comparison and peer pressure, but Caster pays employees according to individual output alone, removing much of the incentive to match a team's overall performance; without face-to-face contact to reinforce that pressure further, it appears to have little effect at all. Experienced colleagues, by contrast, seem able to give newcomers efficient, targeted guidance precisely when it is needed, a benefit that requires no visible display of productivity and, the study suggests, works better with less routine interruption rather than more. For managers, the practical implication is straightforward even if it runs against instinct: rather than scattering top performers across teams in the hope that their example will lift everyone else, organisations may do better to pair newcomers deliberately with longer-serving colleagues, while giving already experienced or highly productive staff more autonomy and fewer scheduled check-ins.
